entries.accessDetail: Bibliographic record reviewed; full text not read in this pass.

entries.title: Allosaurus fragilis: a revised osteology
entries.body: Madsen’s monograph is the baseline for the Cleveland-Lloyd sample. It documents dozens of individuals and the quarry’s taphonomy; the cause of the accumulation remains an interpretation.
entries.accessDetail: Metadata and abstract reviewed; full text not read.

entries.title: Cranial design and function in a large theropod dinosaur
entries.body: Rayfield and colleagues modelled the skull and jaw. The results constrain bite function; they do not record hunting behaviour.
entries.accessDetail: Metadata and abstract reviewed; full text not read.

entries.title: High frequencies of theropod bite marks provide evidence for feeding, scavenging, and possible cannibalism
entries.body: Drumheller and colleagues document direct feeding traces at Mygatt-Moore, including marks on Allosaurus bones. The traces establish carcass utilization, not the hunting method.
entries.accessDetail: Abstract reviewed; full text not read.

entries.title: Original description: The Ankylosauridae, a new family of armored dinosaurs
entries.body: Brown’s 1908 description is the name-bearing account. The original material was incomplete; later specimens and comparisons supply the armour and tail-club anatomy.
entries.accessDetail: Bibliographic record reviewed; full text not read in this pass.

entries.title: Redescription of Ankylosaurus magniventris
entries.body: Carpenter’s redescription is the main anatomical reference for the skull, osteoderms and tail club. It also makes clear how small the sampled hypodigm is.
entries.accessDetail: Metadata and abstract reviewed; full text not read.

entries.title: Tail-club impact mechanics
entries.body: Arbour’s modelling estimates the forces a club could generate. The model supports a defensive function but cannot demonstrate that the animal used the club in combat.
entries.accessDetail: Abstract reviewed; full text not read.

entries.title: Original description: Baryonyx, a remarkable new theropod dinosaur
entries.body: Charig and Milner’s 1986 announcement established the name and the significance of the Smokejacks skeleton. The full monograph followed in 1997.
entries.accessDetail: Bibliographic record reviewed; full text not read in this pass.

entries.title: The osteology of Baryonyx walkeri
entries.body: The 1997 monograph describes the skull, postcranium and associated fish remains. It is the primary source for the diet and manual-claw evidence.
entries.accessDetail: Metadata and abstract reviewed; full text not read.

entries.title: A long-snouted predatory dinosaur from Africa and the evolution of spinosaurids
entries.body: Sereno and colleagues compared Baryonyx with African spinosaurids. The comparison supports the spinosaurid affinities of Baryonyx and the convergent long-snout anatomy.
entries.accessDetail: Metadata and abstract reviewed; full text not read.

entries.title: Original description: Brachiosaurus altithorax, the largest known dinosaur
entries.body: Riggs’ 1903 description is the name-bearing account. The holotype is a partial postcranial skeleton, so the skull and many proportional details come from referred material.
entries.accessDetail: Bibliographic record reviewed; full text not read in this pass.

entries.title: A re-evaluation of Brachiosaurus and Giraffatitan
entries.body: Taylor’s analysis separates the African species into Giraffatitan and restricts Brachiosaurus altithorax to the North American holotype and close material. The separation is anatomical and phylogenetic.
entries.accessDetail: Metadata and abstract reviewed; full text not read.

entries.title: The skull of Brachiosaurus and its attribution
entries.body: D’Emic and Carrano redescribe the referred skull material and review its bearing on brachiosaurid anatomy. The attribution remains an inference because the holotype lacks a skull.
entries.accessDetail: Metadata and abstract reviewed; full text not read.

deinonychus.note: The type, foot, tail and growth literature was rechecked. The MESOZO Discoveries entry for YPM 5205 has been corrected: the holotype is a pair of feet, not a whole skeleton. No feather impressions are known from this species.
deinonychus.specimenStatus: Holotype YPM 5205 (complete left pes, incomplete right pes), Yale Peabody Museum. Verified in Ostrom (1969); the Discoveries archive entry has been corrected to match the original description.

entries.title: Original description: Osteology of Deinonychus antirrhopus
entries.body: Ostrom’s 1969 monograph is the name-bearing description. It records YPM 5205 as the type and documents the specialised second toe, stiffened tail and lightly built limbs.
entries.accessDetail: Repository full text consulted for the type and anatomical passages; not read cover to cover.

entries.title: Growth-related variation in the Deinonychus sample
entries.body: Parsons and Parsons document shape changes through ontogeny and caution against identifying isolated bones from size alone.
entries.accessDetail: Abstract and metadata reviewed; full text not read.

entries.title: The Tenontosaurus–Deinonychus associations
entries.body: Maxwell and Ostrom describe the association and its taphonomy. The evidence shows feeding or carcass association, not coordinated pack killing.
entries.accessDetail: Metadata and abstract reviewed; full text not read.

entries.title: Re-evaluating cooperative pack hunting
entries.body: Roach and Brinkman review the behavioural inference and argue that the evidence for gregarious pack hunting is weaker than often claimed.
entries.accessDetail: Metadata and abstract reviewed; full text not read.

giganotosaurus.note: The Candeleros holotype and braincase literature were rechecked. MUCPv-CH-1 is the type; size estimates vary widely and no direct prey or behavioural evidence is known.
giganotosaurus.specimenStatus: Holotype MUCPv-CH-1 (partial skull, axial skeleton, pelvis and hindlimbs), Museo de la Universidad Nacional del Comahue, El Chocón collection; the braincase is reported as hosted at the Museo Ernesto Bachmann. Verified in Coria & Salgado (1995), Coria & Currie (2002) and Paulina-Carabajal & Nieto (2020). No verified public item-level catalogue record was located in this pass. The type number and repository are recorded from the original description or a modern revision; this is a documentation gap, not evidence that the specimen is uncurated.

entries.title: Original description: A new giant carnivorous dinosaur from the Cretaceous of Patagonia
entries.body: Coria and Salgado name Giganotosaurus carolinii from MUCPv-CH-1 and describe the partial skull and postcranium.
entries.accessDetail: Metadata and abstract reviewed; full text not read.

entries.title: The braincase of Giganotosaurus
entries.body: Coria and Currie describe the braincase and its bearing on theropod relationships and body size.
entries.accessDetail: Abstract and type description reviewed; full text not read.

entries.title: CT scans of the brain and inner ear
entries.body: Paulina-Carabajal and Nieto reconstruct the brain cavity and inner ear from the holotype braincase. The endocast is not preserved brain tissue.
entries.accessDetail: Abstract and metadata reviewed; full text not read.

entries.title: Body-size estimates and their limits
entries.body: Mazzetta and colleagues provide one set of mass estimates. Different methods and reconstructions produce a wide range, and no complete skeleton is known.
entries.accessDetail: Metadata and abstract reviewed; museum summary reviewed.

stegosaurus.note: Batch 5 added a claim-level review and a specimen-status record. Holotype USNM 4934 (nearly complete skeleton), Smithsonian National Museum of Natural History. Access limits are recorded on each entry; no dedicated MESOZO Discoveries page was invented where none exists.
stegosaurus.specimenStatus: Holotype USNM 4934 (nearly complete skeleton), Smithsonian National Museum of Natural History. Referred specimen NHMUK PV R36730 (articulated skeleton), Natural History Museum, London. Both have dedicated MESOZO Discoveries entries.

entries.title: Holotype: USNM 4934
entries.body: The name-bearing skeleton is nearly complete and preserves the skull, axial skeleton, limbs and armour. It is the basis of Stegosaurus stenops and of much early work on stegosaur armour.
entries.accessDetail: Smithsonian specimen record and Marsh’s published description excerpt inspected.

entries.title: Referred specimen: NHMUK PV R36730
entries.body: The “Sophie” specimen preserves much of the skeleton and armour in articulation, including the plates and tail spikes. It documents one individual’s armour arrangement.
entries.accessDetail: Abstract and metadata reviewed; full text not read.

entries.title: Plate and spike function
entries.body: The plates are osteoderms in two alternating rows; the tail bears four spikes. Display, thermoregulation and species recognition remain competing functional hypotheses.
entries.accessDetail: Abstract and metadata reviewed; full text not read.
